markerNotes: Explain requires a causal chain: trade and migration brought the cult, its appeal to sailors and traders explains its popularity, and the rebuilt temple shows its following.
The top band requires a conclusion about cultural contact as exchange and adaptation, not a simple transfer of religion.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that the Romans adopted Isis without explaining how the cult travelled.
Describing the temple as Egyptian in every respect, without noting the Roman architecture and local context.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains the routes by which the cult reached Pompeii, the adaptation of Egyptian elements, and what the presence of the cult reveals about cultural contact as exchange.
4 marks: Explains the routes and the adaptation of the cult with relevant evidence.
3 marks: Explains the arrival of the cult with some evidence, but without the link to cultural contact.
2 marks: Identifies a route or a feature of the cult with minimal explanation.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about Isis or Pompeii.

sampleAnswers.answer: The cult of Isis reached Pompeii through the networks of trade and migration that linked Italy with Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean. Egyptian and Greek merchants, sailors and freedmen brought the worship of Isis from the ports of the eastern Mediterranean, and the cult was attractive to people who wanted a personal relationship with a goddess who promised protection to sailors and traders. The Temple of Isis at Pompeii, which was damaged in the earthquake of 62 CE and then rebuilt, shows that the cult had a substantial following and enough wealth to sustain a large sanctuary. The Egyptian elements of the cult were adapted to Roman tastes, so that the shrine combined Egyptian-style imagery with Roman architecture and local customs. The presence of Isis therefore reveals cultural contact as a process of exchange and adaptation, rather than a simple transfer of foreign religion. Its followers included people of different origins and status, which shows that the cult had social as well as religious appeal. It also shows how Roman cities could absorb new religious practices while keeping their own civic cults. Other Egyptian cults, such as that of Serapis, also reached Italian cities, which suggests a wider pattern of religious exchange.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: explains the routes (trade, migration, sailors), the appeal of the cult, the rebuilt temple as evidence of a following, the adaptation of Egyptian elements, and the conclusion that cultural contact was exchange.

sampleAnswers.answer: Isis worship came to Italy from Egypt through merchants and sailors. The temple at Pompeii was an important sanctuary and it was rebuilt after the earthquake. This shows that Romans were interested in Egyptian religion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the arrival through merchants and notes the temple, but the claim about Romans' interest is not developed and the link to cultural contact is missing. It sits in the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The worship of Isis came from Egypt.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A basic statement with no explanation of how the cult reached Pompeii, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student visiting Pompeii notices the Temple of Isis, which was damaged in the earthquake of 62 CE and then rebuilt. The student is asked to use this to explain how Egyptian religion spread in the Roman world.

dotPoints.description: A study of at least ONE significant site relating to trade, such as a shipwreck or port

prompts.question: Describe the cargo of the Uluburun shipwreck and what it reveals about trade in the Late Bronze Age eastern Mediterranean.
markerNotes: Describe needs specific categories with accurate detail: copper and tin as oxhide and bun-shaped ingots, glass ingots, elephant ivory, resin and ceramics.
The explanation of what the cargo reveals (an interconnected Late Bronze Age network moving bulk and luxury goods) is what earns the top band.
commonStudentErrors: Dating the Uluburun wreck to the Roman period, more than a thousand years too late.
Describing the cargo as copper alone, without the tin that made the copper useful as bronze.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes the main categories of cargo (copper and tin ingots, glass, ivory, resin, ceramics) with accurate detail and explains what the cargo reveals about Late Bronze Age trade.
3 marks: Describes several categories of cargo accurately, with some explanation of their significance.
2 marks: Describes two categories of cargo accurately.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about the wreck.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Uluburun shipwreck, dating to about 1300 BCE, carried a remarkable cargo of raw materials and finished goods. Its most important cargo was copper, in the form of oxhide ingots, and tin, which was needed to make bronze, so the ship was carrying the two components of the alloy in large quantities. The wreck also contained glass ingots, ivory, ebony, resin and ceramics from several regions, including Canaanite jars and Mycenaean pottery. Some of the cargo was prestigious, such as the exotic materials that suggest an elite or royal market for luxury goods. Taken together, the cargo shows that the Late Bronze Age eastern Mediterranean had an interconnected trade network that moved both bulk raw materials and luxury goods over long distances, and that the shipwreck is evidence of a voyage that linked several cultures. The wreck was found off the southern coast of Turkey in 1982, and the study of its cargo continues to show the scale of this trade.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: describes the main categories of cargo with accurate detail, and explains that together they reveal an interconnected Late Bronze Age trade network in bulk and luxury goods.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Uluburun ship carried copper and tin, which are used to make bronze. It also had glass and ivory.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate items, but no account of what the cargo reveals about trade, and the categories are not developed. It fits the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Uluburun shipwreck is an old wreck from Turkey.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement about the wreck with no cargo detail, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A Year 11 student is using a hypothetical museum panel, invented for this exercise, about a shipwreck found off the southern coast of Turkey in 1982 by a sponge diver. The panel notes that the ship was carrying raw materials from several regions.

prompts.question: Explain how the harbour at Portus, built beside Ostia, supported the supply of grain and trade goods to Rome in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE.
markerNotes: Explain needs a chain: large ships could not reach Rome, so Portus let them unload, goods moved by river to the city, and the state invested to keep the supply reliable.
Marks go to the development over time (Claudius, then Trajan) and to the link between harbour infrastructure and the city's food supply.
commonStudentErrors: Describing Portus as a port for Ostia only, without its role in supplying Rome.
Stating that Portus was built by Trajan, which ignores Claudius's harbour.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains how Portus worked as a port (harbour basins, unloading, storage, transfer to river craft) and how it supported Rome's grain supply, with evidence of its development and state investment.
5 marks: Explains the function of the harbour and its role in the grain supply, with relevant evidence.
4 marks: Explains the harbour's function with some reference to Rome's supply.
3 marks: Describes the harbour with limited explanation of its role.
2 marks: Identifies one feature of the harbour with minimal explanation.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about Portus or Ostia.

sampleAnswers.answer: Portus, the harbour built beside Ostia, was designed to solve the problem that the coastline near the Tiber mouth was poorly suited to large ships, so it allowed grain and other goods to be unloaded safely for transport to Rome. Claudius began the harbour in the 40s CE, creating a sheltered basin protected by breakwaters so that large merchant ships could anchor and unload their cargoes, protected from the dangers of the open coast. The project was costly and technically demanding, which is why it required imperial sponsorship rather than private investment. Trajan later extended the harbour with a second, hexagonal basin, which increased its capacity and protected shipping from storms. Grain shipped from Egypt and North Africa was transferred to smaller river craft and carried up the Tiber to Rome, and the port complex included warehouses and facilities for storage. The site therefore supported the trade that fed the capital, linking the sea routes of the Mediterranean with the city's food supply. Its development over time shows how the Roman state invested heavily in port infrastructure to secure the grain supply of Rome, one of the largest cities of the ancient world. Its role also depended on the Tiber, whose traffic had to be managed, so the harbour system linked open sea, river and the city's storage facilities in one connected network. Portus therefore shows the grain supply as a matter of imperial policy, not merely of private commerce.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: explains the harbour's function (sheltered basins for large ships, transfer to river craft, warehouses), its role in Rome's grain supply, and the investment over time by Claudius and Trajan.

sampleAnswers.answer: Portus was built by Claudius to help large ships unload near Rome. Trajan added another basin later. Grain came from Egypt and was taken up the Tiber to Rome in smaller boats. The harbour had warehouses for storing goods before they reached the city, which made the grain supply more reliable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the function and the river transfer, and links the warehouses to supply, but the reasons for the state's investment and the wider trade are not explained. It sits in the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Portus was a harbour near Rome.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no function or evidence, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student is studying a site relating to trade in the Roman world and has a plan of the harbour complex showing the basin built under Claudius and the later basin added by Trajan. The student is asked to explain how the harbour fed the city rather than simply describe its layout.

topics.name: Core study: Cities of Vesuvius – Pompeii and Herculaneum

dotPoints.description: The geographical setting and natural features of Campania

prompts.question: Identify two natural features of the Campanian landscape that shaped the settlement of Pompeii and Herculaneum.
markerNotes: Two different features are needed. Vesuvius and the volcanic soil it produced are linked, so they should be counted as one feature unless they are separately explained.
The link to the cities is what turns a geographical fact into a historical answer.
commonStudentErrors: Naming Italy or the Mediterranean as a natural feature. These are too general to shape the settlements.
Giving Vesuvius and its eruption as two separate natural features. The eruption is an event, not a feature of the landscape.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies two distinct natural features of Campania (for example Vesuvius, volcanic soils, the Bay of Naples or the Sarno River) and links at least one to the cities.
1 mark: Identifies one natural feature without linking it to the cities.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two natural features of Campania shaped Pompeii and Herculaneum: Mount Vesuvius, whose eruptions later buried the cities, and the fertile volcanic soil that supported farming. Both are central to their geographical setting.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: two distinct features (Vesuvius and the volcanic soils), each linked to the cities through settlement, agriculture and burial, and placed within the geographical setting.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mount Vesuvius is a volcano near the cities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One feature with only a location given, and no link to how it shaped the settlement, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is labelling a sketch map of the Bay of Naples for a revision booklet. The map must show the features that shaped where the towns were built.

prompts.question: Explain how the volcanic soils and coastal position of Campania shaped the economic life of Pompeii and Herculaneum before 79 CE.
markerNotes: Explain needs the causal chain: fertile soil produced crops and wine, which were sold locally and by sea because of the coast.
The top band rewards seeing agriculture and sea trade as one economy, not as two separate facts.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the soils as fertile without saying what they produced or why it mattered economically.
Describing the cities as purely agricultural and ignoring the role of the sea and the rivers.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains how the soils and the coastal position each shaped economic activity, and how together they gave the towns a diverse economy, with specific evidence.
4 marks: Explains the economic effects of both features with relevant evidence, with limited linking between them.
3 marks: Identifies both features and their economic uses without explaining how they combined.
2 marks: Identifies one feature and its economic use.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about Campania's geography.

sampleAnswers.answer: The volcanic soils of Campania gave Pompeii and Herculaneum an unusually productive agricultural base, because the earth derived from ancient eruptions was rich in minerals and held water well. The fertile plain supported vineyards, olive groves and grain, and the wine and oil of the region were sold through local markets and sent by sea. The coastal position of the two cities made them important points for maritime trade, since ships could load and unload at ports close to the Bay of Naples, and the Sarno River gave Pompeii access to the coast for river traffic. This combination of agriculture and sea trade gave the towns a diverse economy, in which farmers, merchants, craftsmen and shipping workers all depended on the landscape. Herculaneum, which sat on the shore, relied even more directly on the sea, with boathouses that show how closely fishing and transport were tied to the town's life. The geography of Campania therefore shaped the economy of both cities well before 79 CE, and its fertile soils and sheltered coast created the wealth that later made their houses so richly decorated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: explains how the volcanic soils produced crops for local and sea markets, how the coastal position created maritime trade, and how the two combined into a diverse economy, with specific evidence (vines, oil, the Sarno, Herculaneum boathouses).

sampleAnswers.answer: Volcanic soils were good for farming, so people grew crops and vines. The cities were near the coast and so could trade. Herculaneum also had boats.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies both features and a use for each, but does not explain how the two combined into an economy. It fits the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Campania had a volcano, which is Vesuvius.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A geographical fact with no economic link, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student is writing a paragraph for an essay on the cities' economies and needs to explain why agriculture and trade were so important to them. The paragraph should link the land and the coast to the way people earned their living.

dotPoints.description: The impact of the eruption of 79 CE on Pompeii and Herculaneum

prompts.question: Distinguish between the impact of the eruption of 79 CE on Pompeii and its impact on Herculaneum, in terms of the processes that buried each city.
markerNotes: Distinguish needs a stated difference at each stage: the process, the speed, the depth of the deposit and the effect on preservation.
Precise terms (pumice fall, pyroclastic surge) earn the top band. Describing either city as covered by lava is a common error.
commonStudentErrors: Describing lava flows at either city. Deaths and burial came from ash fall and pyroclastic surges.
Treating both cities as buried in the same way, with only the depth different.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Distinguishes the two processes (pumice and ash fall at Pompeii, pyroclastic surges at Herculaneum) and explains how each produced a different impact on the city and on its survival.
3 marks: Distinguishes the two processes accurately, with limited explanation of their effects.
2 marks: Describes the process at each site without fully distinguishing their impact.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about the eruption.

sampleAnswers.answer: The eruption of 79 CE affected Pompeii and Herculaneum in different ways, and the impact depended on the processes that buried each city. At Pompeii the main process was a fall of pumice and ash, which accumulated over many hours and collapsed roofs under its weight, so people who stayed in the city could die when buildings failed, while the town was gradually buried under several metres of material. At Herculaneum the impact was more sudden: pyroclastic surges, fast-moving currents of hot gas and debris, swept down the slope and buried the town under a much deeper and more compact deposit. This compact deposit preserved organic material, including wooden objects and carbonised food, to a greater degree than at Pompeii. The difference in process therefore explains why the two cities survived in different states and why their evidence differs. The Herculaneum record is therefore strongest in perishable goods, while the Pompeii record is strongest in the layout of streets and buildings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: distinguishes the pumice and ash fall from the pyroclastic surges, and explains the different impact on the people, the depth of burial and the preservation of organic material.

sampleAnswers.answer: At Pompeii, the city was buried by pumice and ash falling from the sky. At Herculaneum, the town was hit by a flow of hot material that buried it more deeply.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the process at each site accurately but does not explain how the difference changed the impact on survival or preservation. It fits the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The eruption destroyed both cities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general claim with no distinction between the two sites, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student is comparing the deposits excavated at the two sites, which show a thick layer of pumice and ash at Pompeii and a deeper, more compact surge deposit at Herculaneum. The student must explain how these different deposits affected what survived at each site.

prompts.question: Discuss the extent to which the eruption of 79 CE caused the decline of Pompeii and Herculaneum, rather than a process that had begun earlier, such as the damage of the earthquake of 62 CE.
markerNotes: Discuss needs a judgement on extent. The strongest answers treat the eruption as the decisive final event, and the earthquake as evidence that decline had already begun.
Use evidence on both sides (the physical scale of the burial, Pliny's account, the 62 CE damage and incomplete repairs), then say which side the evidence favours and why.
commonStudentErrors: Treating the eruption as the only cause without considering the evidence for earlier decline.
Asserting that Pompeii was in decline without citing the 62 CE earthquake or the state of repairs.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Discusses the extent to which the eruption caused decline, weighing the physical scale of the eruption against evidence of earlier decline (such as the 62 CE earthquake and incomplete repairs), and reaches a supported judgement.
5-6 marks: Discusses the eruption's role and the evidence for earlier decline, with a partly supported judgement.
4 marks: Describes the eruption's effects and the earthquake, with some discussion of their relationship.
2-3 marks: Identifies relevant events or effects with limited discussion.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about the eruption or the cities.

sampleAnswers.answer: The eruption of 79 CE was the decisive event in the destruction of both cities, but the extent to which it caused their decline depends on how the evidence is weighed. The strongest case for the eruption as the cause is the physical scale of the event. Pompeii was buried under pumice and ash to a depth of several metres, and Herculaneum was overwhelmed by surges that buried it more deeply, so both sites were abandoned and their populations were lost or displaced. Pliny the Younger's account of the eruption, written decades later, shows that contemporaries saw it as a sudden catastrophe rather than a gradual decline. However, the argument for continuity is also important. Pompeii had been struck by a severe earthquake in 62 CE, and the evidence from the years before 79 CE suggests that repairs to public buildings were incomplete when the eruption occurred. This suggests that the city's recovery was already uneven, and that the eruption accelerated a decline that had begun with the earthquake. At Herculaneum the evidence for earlier damage is less clear, so a continuity argument is harder to make there. Testing that argument requires dating the repairs precisely, and the scholarly debate about the state of the buildings in 79 CE shows how much depends on interpreting incomplete evidence. Pliny's letters, though valuable, were written by an observer at Misenum who was not in Pompeii and who described the eruption rather than the condition of the cities beforehand. Each side therefore rests on inference from the physical remains, which is why the judgement must remain qualified. The historian must therefore distinguish between the eruption as an immediate cause and the eruption as the final stage of a longer process. On balance, the eruption was the decisive cause of the end of both cities, but the earthquake of 62 CE is a strong reason to treat decline as a process rather than a single event.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: weighs the physical scale of the eruption and Pliny's account against the continuity argument from the 62 CE earthquake and incomplete repairs, distinguishes immediate from long-term cause, and reaches a supported judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: The eruption was the main reason both cities ended. Pompeii was covered in ash and pumice, and Herculaneum was buried by a surge, so people could not return. Pliny the Younger's letters describe the eruption as a sudden catastrophe. However, Pompeii had an earthquake in 62 CE, so some people think it was already in decline. The eruption probably caused most of the damage.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate points, but the verdict that the eruption probably caused most of the damage is asserted without weighing the evidence for earlier decline. The discussion is one-sided and underdeveloped, so it sits in the 5-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The eruption of 79 CE destroyed Pompeii and Herculaneum. Some people say there was an earthquake before that.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two accurate statements with no discussion of the extent of the eruption's role, so it fits the 2-mark band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is challenged by a classmate who argues that Pompeii was already declining before 79 CE and that the eruption only completed a process that had begun. The student must decide how far the evidence supports this view.

subTopics.name: Source analysis: interpreting the evidence for life in Pompeii and Herculaneum

dotPoints.description: The nature, range, value and limitations of sources about Pompeii and Herculaneum, including art, buildings, organic remains and writing

prompts.question: Classify each of the four items in the scenario as art, buildings, organic remains or writing, and give a brief reason for each classification.
markerNotes: Classification depends on what the item is (its material, its purpose and the evidence it gives), not on how it looks.
A brief reason shows the classification is deliberate. For example, writing because the notice communicates a message to the public in text.
commonStudentErrors: Classifying the election notice as art because it is painted, when its purpose is to communicate written content.
Placing the loaf in buildings or art because it was found inside a house.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Classifies all four items correctly, with a reason for at least two of them.
2 marks: Classifies three of the four items correctly.
1 mark: Classifies one or two items correctly.

sampleAnswers.answer: The carbonised loaf from a Herculaneum house is organic remains, preserved by heat and ash. The wall painting of a fish market is art, since its purpose is decorative. The painted election notice from Pompeii is writing, because it conveys a public message. The floor plan of a house with a peristyle garden is evidence from buildings, recording the layout of a domestic space. Each classification shows what the item can reveal about life in the cities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: classifies all four items correctly, with a reason for each, linking the classification to the kind of information each item gives.

sampleAnswers.answer: The loaf is organic remains and the fish market painting is art. The house plan is buildings. The election notice is art because it is painted on a wall.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Three of the four items are classified correctly. The election notice is misclassified because the medium was used instead of the purpose of the item. It fits the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The loaf is organic remains.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One item classified correctly with no reasons, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student has four items from a hypothetical museum display (invented for this task): a carbonised loaf found in a Herculaneum house, a wall painting of a fish market, a painted election notice from Pompeii, and the floor plan of a house with a peristyle garden. The student must give a reason for each classification.

prompts.question: Evaluate the value and limitations of art, buildings, organic remains and writing as sources for everyday life in Pompeii and Herculaneum.
markerNotes: Evaluate needs a judgement on reliability and usefulness. Each source needs a value and a limitation tied to the question of everyday life.
The strongest answers judge the sources against each other, for example by noting that organic remains show everyday practice while art shows what the wealthy wanted to display.
commonStudentErrors: Describing each source type without saying what it can or cannot show about everyday life.
Treating writing as the most reliable evidence simply because it is written, without considering who wrote it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Evaluates the value and limitations of each source type for everyday life, weighs their reliability against one another, and reaches a supported judgement on their combined use.
6 marks: Evaluates the value and limitations of most source types with supported reasons, reaching a partly developed judgement.
5 marks: Explains the value and limitations of several source types with some evaluation.
3-4 marks: Describes the value or limitations of some source types with limited evaluation.
2 marks: Identifies source types with minimal comment on value or limitations.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about sources.

sampleAnswers.answer: Each type of source offers a distinct value for understanding everyday life in Pompeii and Herculaneum, and each has limitations that the historian must acknowledge. Art, mainly wall paintings and mosaics, is valuable because it shows domestic scenes, religious images and the tastes of wealthy householders, such as the scenes of banquets and mythology in elite houses. Its limitation is that it was produced for a patron or a market and often idealises life, so it cannot be taken as a simple record of ordinary experience. Buildings offer a more reliable record of how space was used, because the arrangement of rooms, shops and workshops reveals the household economy and the division of public and private life. Their limitation is that many buildings were altered or repaired before 79 CE, and that their function can be inferred only from their layout, so the evidence needs to be interpreted with care. Organic remains, including carbonised bread, figs and wooden objects found at Herculaneum, give a rare insight into diet and material culture, and they show the value of the surge deposits. Their limitation is that such remains are unevenly preserved, so they cannot be used to reconstruct the full range of food consumed in either city. Writing, including graffiti, election notices and the wax tablets of the banker Caecilius Iucundus, gives direct voices from ordinary people, which is a major value because it reveals opinions and transactions. Its limitation is that most surviving texts were written by men, and that the literate minority was small, so the writing reflects a narrow section of society. Taken together, the sources are most valuable when used in combination: art and buildings show what the wealthy wanted to display, while organic remains and writing provide evidence of everyday practice. The historian must therefore weigh each source by its purpose, its preservation and its authorship.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: evaluates the value and limitation of each of the four source types, weighs them against one another (what the wealthy displayed against everyday practice), and reaches a supported judgement on combined use.

sampleAnswers.answer: Art shows the wealthy and their tastes, such as banquet scenes, but it is idealised. Buildings show how houses were arranged and used, which helps understand daily life. Organic remains from Herculaneum include food, so we know what people ate. Writing like graffiti is useful because it shows what ordinary people thought, but it is not very common. These sources all have some value and some limitations, so they should be used together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a value and a limitation for most sources, but the judgement that they should be used together is not argued against their relative reliability. It sits in the 5-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Art and buildings are sources about Pompeii and Herculaneum. Writing is also a source.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies source types with no comment on value or limitations, so it fits the 2-mark band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is writing an essay on everyday life in the cities and must judge which kinds of evidence are most reliable. The essay must weigh the usefulness of each kind of evidence against its limits.

dotPoints.description: Social organisation, including men, women, freedmen, freedwomen and enslaved people

prompts.question: Describe the social position of freedmen and freedwomen in Pompeii, using evidence from the houses of wealthy freed families.
markerNotes: Describe needs both sides of the position: the mobility of freedmen (wealth, houses, decoration) and their continuing dependence on former owners.
The House of the Vettii is the expected example. Naming it and linking its decoration to status earns the specific evidence mark.
commonStudentErrors: Describing freedmen as fully equal to free-born citizens.
Writing about enslaved people when the question asks about freedmen and freedwomen.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes the position of freedmen and freedwomen with specific evidence from freed families, and explains the combination of upward mobility and continuing dependence.
3 marks: Describes the position with specific evidence, with limited analysis.
2 marks: Describes the status of freedmen or gives one example accurately.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about social groups in Pompeii.

sampleAnswers.answer: Freedmen and freedwomen occupied a distinctive place in the social organisation of Pompeii. Many had been enslaved and were freed by their owners, and they were able to build wealth through trade, manufacturing and commerce, so some became prosperous enough to own large houses and to commission elaborate wall paintings. The House of the Vettii, which belonged to freed brothers, shows how a freedman family could display wealth and status through decorative schemes that rivalled those of the old elite. The paintings and the house plan together signal that the family wanted to be seen as part of the civic elite, even though legal rights were not identical. Yet freed status carried legal and social limitations, because freedmen remained tied to their former masters through obligations of service and respect, and the enslaved people who worked in these households had no legal standing of their own. The position of freedmen therefore combined upward mobility with continuing dependence on the families they had once served.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: describes the mobility of freed families using the House of the Vettii, and explains the continuing obligations to former owners and the lack of legal standing of enslaved people.

sampleAnswers.answer: Freedmen were people who had been slaves and were then freed. The House of the Vettii was owned by freedmen and was richly decorated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate definition and one example, but no analysis of the position or its limitations. It fits the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Enslaved people were not free in Pompeii.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement about enslaved people rather than freedmen, so it does not answer the question and earns only the 1-mark band.

prompts.scenario: A student is studying the House of the Vettii, a large Pompeian house decorated with frescoes, and is told that its owners were freedmen who had once been enslaved. The student is asked to use this house to describe how freed families fitted into the town's society.

prompts.question: Interpret the hypothetical graffito described in the scenario and explain what it suggests about relationships between enslaved people, freedmen and their owners in Pompeii.
markerNotes: Interpret means explaining what the text implies, not restating it. The implication about manumission and the household's interests is what earns the marks.
A top answer treats the graffito as one hypothetical source and says what it cannot show, such as how common such cases were.
commonStudentErrors: Paraphrasing the graffito without interpreting it.
Generalising from one hypothetical text to all enslaved people in Pompeii.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Interprets the graffito as evidence of manumission and of freedmen's economic roles, weighs its reliability as a single source, and explains what it reveals about relationships between enslaved people and owners.
4 marks: Interprets the graffito with relevant explanation and some evaluation of its reliability.
3 marks: Explains the main meaning of the graffito with limited evaluation.
2 marks: Paraphrases the graffito with minimal interpretation.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about the graffito.

sampleAnswers.answer: The hypothetical graffito suggests that manumission, or freeing, was one route by which enslaved people could move into a new social position in Pompeii. The fact that the owner's decision is recorded on a public wall indicates that the household was willing to display its generosity, and that the change of status was socially meaningful rather than private. The graffito also implies that a freed man could be given responsibility, such as running a shop, which shows that freedmen could take on economic roles that kept them connected to the household. Such roles made the freedman valuable to the owner, because his profits and loyalty benefited the household. However, the text is a single hypothetical source, and it cannot show whether all manumissions were this positive or how common they were. The owner may have benefited from the arrangement, since a freedman remained bound by obligations to the former master, and many enslaved people had no such prospect. The evidence therefore suggests that social relationships in Pompeii were flexible at the margins but still based on the owner's power over the household.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: interprets the graffito as evidence of manumission and of freedmen's economic roles, explains the owner's interests, and evaluates the reliability of a single hypothetical source.

sampleAnswers.answer: The graffito shows that some enslaved people were freed. A freed slave could run a shop for their former owner. This shows that owners could be generous, but it probably was not common.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the main meaning and draws a reasonable inference about generosity, but the claim that such cases were uncommon is unsupported and the evaluation is limited. It sits in the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The graffito is about a freed slave.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement that does not interpret the graffito, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A hypothetical wall graffito (invented for this task, not a real inscription) records that a named enslaved man has been freed by his owner and will now run a shop for the household. A student is asked to consider what it reveals about the household.

dotPoints.description: Local political life, including magistrates and elections

prompts.question: State the title of the two chief magistrates of Pompeii and one duty they performed.
markerNotes: Use the correct Latin title and its meaning: the duoviri iure dicundo were the two chief magistrates, with judicial power.
The duty should be specific (presiding over the courts) rather than general (running the town).
commonStudentErrors: Using consul for the Pompeian chief magistrates, which confuses the town's offices with the Roman consulship.
Stating a duty without naming the office it belonged to.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: States the title of the chief magistrates correctly (duoviri iure dicundo) and gives one correct duty.
1 mark: States the title correctly without a duty, or gives a correct duty without the title.

sampleAnswers.answer: The two chief magistrates of Pompeii were the duoviri iure dicundo, who presided over the courts. They were chosen in annual elections and held the highest executive power in the town.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: gives the correct title, a specific duty (presiding over the courts), and accurate context on annual elections and executive power.

sampleAnswers.answer: The chief magistrates were called duoviri.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States the title with no duty, so it earns the 1-mark band.

prompts.question: Explain how elections worked in Pompeii and what the painted election notices reveal about political competition in the town.
markerNotes: Explain needs the mechanism (annual elections for the magistrates, notices urging voters) and the significance (patronage, endorsement and a limited franchise).
The top band weighs openness against exclusion, using the notices as evidence of both.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the notices as official government announcements rather than campaign material.
Claiming that all Pompeians could vote, which ignores the restricted franchise.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains the election process and the use of notices, analyses what the notices reveal about patronage, endorsement and competition, and assesses the limits on political participation.
4 marks: Explains the process and the notices with analysis of competition or patronage.
3 marks: Describes elections and notices, with some explanation of their purpose.
2 marks: Identifies one feature of elections or notices.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about political life in Pompeii.

sampleAnswers.answer: Elections in Pompeii were held each year for the magistrates, and candidates ran their campaigns publicly on the walls of the town. Supporters painted notices that named a candidate and urged voters to elect him, often adding the name of a trade association or neighbourhood group that endorsed him. The notices show that political life was organised around patronage and local networks rather than around programmes, and that candidates needed the support of wealthy men, guilds and neighbourhood groups to win. The competition was intense, but it was limited to adult male citizens, and in practice to the freeborn and propertied men who could stand for office, so the political life of the town was closed to most of its inhabitants. Women and the enslaved were excluded from the formal process, although they were affected by its outcomes. The notices therefore reveal both the openness and the restrictions of local politics in Pompeii, and the way that elections were a form of public display for the candidate and his supporters. The notices also show that candidates relied on repeated appeals, so the election season was a visible contest rather than a quiet process of appointment, and the walls of the town became a shared arena for political argument.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: explains the annual election process and the notices, analyses patronage and endorsement as the basis of competition, and assesses the restricted franchise against the openness of the campaigns.

sampleAnswers.answer: Elections happened every year and candidates put up notices on the walls asking people to vote for them. Some notices were from guilds. This shows that people were involved in politics.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the notices and their endorsement, but does not explain the competition or the limits on participation. It sits in the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Elections were held in Pompeii.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no process or evidence, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A hypothetical summary of a wall notice (invented for this task) names a candidate for aedile and says that a local trade association supports him. The student is asked to use this to explain the political culture of the town.

dotPoints.description: Economic activities, including commerce, industries and occupations

prompts.question: Deduce the main economic activities of Pompeii from the evidence of its workshops, shops and amphorae.
markerNotes: Deduce means reasoning from the evidence to a conclusion. Naming the fullery is description. Saying what its basins imply about scale and organisation is deduction.
Strong answers separate production (fulling, garum) from retail (bakeries, shops) and draw a conclusion about the balance between them.
commonStudentErrors: Listing workshops without explaining what they reveal about the economy.
Deducing that all Pompeian workshops were run by enslaved workers, which the evidence does not establish.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Deduces several economic activities from specific types of evidence (fullery, bakeries, garum production, amphorae), explains what each reveals about commerce and industry, and reaches a conclusion about the economy.
4 marks: Deduces several activities from specific evidence, with explanation of their significance.
3 marks: Identifies activities from the evidence with limited deduction.
2 marks: Lists evidence of activities without linking it to the economy.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about Pompeii's economy.

sampleAnswers.answer: The economic activities indicated by the workshops and shops of Pompeii point to a diverse local economy based on manufacturing, food production and commerce. The fullers' basins and treading areas show that cloth was finished on a commercial scale, since fulling required a steady supply of water and urine, so it was an established industry rather than a household task. The bakeries, with their mills and ovens, show that much of the population relied on bread produced for sale. The garum shops and amphorae point to a substantial trade in processed food and drink, some exported beyond the region. The occupations shown by this evidence were concentrated among artisans and small traders, many of them freed people. Taken together, the evidence shows that commerce and small-scale industries formed the core of the local economy, supplemented by agriculture in the surrounding countryside.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: deduces several activities from specific evidence (fullery basins, bakery mills and ovens, garum and amphorae), explains what each implies about scale and organisation, and concludes about the balance of commerce and industry.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii had many shops and workshops. There was a fullery, which cleaned clothes, and bakeries that made bread. There was also trade in wine and fish sauce, which was sold in amphorae. So the town had a lot of business.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the activities from the evidence, but the deduction stops at general business activity and does not reason about scale or organisation. It fits the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii had shops.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no evidence or deduction, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student is shown a hypothetical street plan (drawn for this task from the types of evidence found at Pompeii) showing a fullery, several bakeries, a shop selling fish sauce and a row of wine-shops. The student must draw conclusions about the local economy.

prompts.question: Describe the form and function of a Pompeian thermopolium, and what it reveals about street-level commerce.
markerNotes: Describe needs the form (masonry counter, jars, street frontage) and the function (sale of food and drink) with accurate detail.
Linking the shop to street-level commerce and to customers who lacked kitchens earns the top band.
commonStudentErrors: Calling the thermopolium a restaurant with tables and chairs, which the form of the shop does not show.
Describing the jars as grain stores rather than containers for wine, water or prepared food.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes both the form (masonry counter, jars) and the function (food and drink sales to passers-by), and explains its place in street-level commerce.
2 marks: Describes the form or the function accurately, with one supporting feature.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about a food shop.

sampleAnswers.answer: A thermopolium was a food and drink shop, typically with a masonry counter that opened onto the street. Its counter contained large jars set into the masonry for holding wine, water and prepared food, so the shop served customers who bought take-away meals and drinks, often standing at the counter. Its activities were a form of retail commerce that brought food and drink to the many people in Pompeii who lived in small apartments or lacked kitchens of their own. Thermopolia are found in large numbers across the town, which shows the importance of street-level commerce in the local economy, and their counters reveal how the business of selling food was built into the fabric of the city.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: describes the counter and jars (form) and the sale of food and drink to passers-by (function), and explains the place of the shop in street-level commerce.

sampleAnswers.answer: A thermopolium was a shop that sold food and drink to passers-by. It had a counter with jars set into it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate on form and function, but does not connect the shop to street-level commerce or the wider economy. It fits the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: A thermopolium was a place where people ate.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement that misses the sale of food and drink and the form of the shop, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A thermopolium (a counter-fronted food and drink shop) is shown in a student's textbook, with a masonry counter containing large jars. The student is asked to describe the shop's form and function, and what it shows about the street.

dotPoints.description: Features and functions of houses

prompts.question: Explain how the features of a typical Pompeian house, such as the atrium, peristyle and street-front shops, reflected the functions of household life, business and display.
markerNotes: Explain needs the link between feature and function: the atrium served reception and display, the peristyle served private life, and the shops served income.
Strong answers note that one house combined domestic, economic and social functions, which is the central point of the question.
commonStudentErrors: Listing features without stating what each one did for the household.
Describing the atrium as a kitchen or bedroom, which confuses its function as a room for reception and display.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains how specific features (atrium, peristyle, tabernae, decoration, lararium) reflected the functions of domestic, economic and social life, and how the layout balanced privacy and display.
5 marks: Explains how several features reflected their functions, with relevant evidence.
4 marks: Describes several features and explains some of their functions.
3 marks: Describes features with limited reference to their functions.
2 marks: Identifies one feature and a use, with minimal explanation.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about Pompeian houses.

sampleAnswers.answer: The features of houses in Pompeii reflected the different functions that a household had to serve. The entrance (fauces) led into the atrium, an open-roofed room with a central pool (impluvium) that collected rainwater, and whose layout let visitors be received and seen by the household, so the atrium functioned as a space of public display and social status. Behind it, the peristyle, a colonnaded garden, gave private space for family life, for dining and for leisure, and the rooms around it show the division between public and private activity. Many houses had shops (tabernae) opening onto the street, which generated income and linked the household to commerce, so the front of a house could be both home and business. Wall paintings and mosaics in reception rooms and dining rooms displayed the owner's taste and wealth, while a lararium, or household shrine, expressed religious devotion within the house. Together these features show that Pompeian houses were designed to serve domestic, economic and social purposes at once, and that their functions shaped the way their spaces were arranged. The layout therefore reveals how the owners balanced privacy and display in a crowded town, and it shows that the same building could hold a family, a workshop and a visible claim to status.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: links specific features (atrium, peristyle, tabernae, decoration, lararium) to domestic, economic and social functions, and explains how the layout balanced privacy and display.

sampleAnswers.answer: A Pompeian house had an atrium, which was a central room with a pool, and a peristyle garden at the back. The atrium was for guests and the peristyle was for the family. Some houses had shops at the front that were rented out to make money. The paintings showed the owner's wealth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes several features and some of their uses, but does not explain how the features together reflected household life, business and display. It fits the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeian houses had gardens and rooms.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no feature explained and no function, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.question: Clarify the relationship between the street-front shops (tabernae) of a Pompeian house and the household that owned it.
markerNotes: Clarify means making the relationship clear: name the connection (an internal door, a shared building) and what it meant for the household.
Two supporting features (street location, access to rooms behind, income) move the answer into the top band.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the shops as separate businesses with no connection to the household.
Treating the tabernae as public buildings owned by the town rather than as part of private houses.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Clarifies the physical and economic relationship between the shops and the household, with at least two supporting features.
2 marks: Describes the shops and their location, with one link to the household.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about shops in Pompeii.

sampleAnswers.answer: The tabernae were shops opening onto the street from the front of many houses in Pompeii. They often connected to the rooms behind through an internal door, so the household and the shop shared one building. This shows that the features of a house, including its shops, served the functions of both domestic life and income. The street-front shop also gave the household a public face, linking its reputation to its trade.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: clarifies the physical link (internal door, shared building) and the economic link (income, household trade), with the street frontage as a public face.

sampleAnswers.answer: The tabernae were shops at the front of houses. They made money for the owners.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate on location and income, but with no link to the household itself. It fits the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Shops were built in Pompeii.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement that does not address the relationship with the household, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student notes that some Pompeian houses have shops opening onto the street, but that the shops are sometimes connected to the house by an internal door. The student must explain how the shop and the household related to each other.

dotPoints.description: Leisure activities, including entertainment and baths

prompts.question: Describe the riot at the amphitheatre of Pompeii in 59 CE and its consequences for the entertainment of the town.
markerNotes: Describe needs the core facts: 59 CE, the amphitheatre, the rivalry with Nuceria, the violence and the Senate's response.
Explaining what the ban meant for entertainment and public order is what earns the top band.
commonStudentErrors: Dating the riot to 79 CE and confusing it with the eruption.
Stating that the ban was permanent, when Tacitus records a ban of ten years.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes the riot (date, setting, parties and violence) accurately from the source, and explains the consequences for entertainment and public order.
3 marks: Describes the riot accurately with one consequence.
2 marks: Describes the riot with limited detail.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about an event at Pompeii.

sampleAnswers.answer: In 59 CE a violent riot broke out at the amphitheatre of Pompeii during a gladiatorial show. According to Tacitus, the fighting began as a quarrel between Pompeians and people from the neighbouring town of Nuceria, and it escalated into the throwing of stones and then bloodshed, with many killed or injured. The Senate responded by banning such gatherings at Pompeii for ten years, and the organiser of the games was punished, which shows how seriously the authorities took the disorder. Tacitus presents the affair as a case in which local pride and the excitement of the crowd combined to produce a disaster, and the ban shows how the state could control the public pleasures of provincial towns. The incident reveals how important entertainment was in the life of the town, and how rivalry between neighbouring communities could turn a show into a violent confrontation that the state had to address.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: describes the riot accurately (date, setting, parties, violence) and explains the consequences for entertainment and public order, including the ten-year ban.

sampleAnswers.answer: There was a riot at the amphitheatre in Pompeii in 59 CE between Pompeians and people from Nuceria. The Senate stopped such gatherings at Pompeii for a while.
sampleAnswers.feedback: An accurate outline of the event and one consequence, with no detail of the violence and no account of what the ban meant for entertainment. It fits the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: A riot happened in Pompeii.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no date, parties or consequence, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student reads Tacitus's account of a riot between people from Pompeii and Nuceria during a gladiatorial show, which the historian records under the year 59 CE. The student must describe the riot and its consequences for the town's shows.

prompts.question: Analyse the role of the public baths in the leisure life of Pompeii, including how bathing related to social status and the wider community.
markerNotes: Analyse needs relationships: how the mix of users and the patronage of wealthy men connected leisure with status and community.
Specific evidence (the Stabian Baths' sequence of rooms, the palaestra, the sections for men and women) carries the top bands.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the baths only as hygiene facilities, which misses their leisure and social role.
Assuming the baths were used only by the wealthy, when the evidence of mixed use and attached shops suggests a wider public.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the baths' role in leisure, including bathing as exercise, conversation and entertainment, the expression of social status, and the creation of community ties, with specific evidence.
5 marks: Analyses two of these roles with relevant evidence and some connection between them.
4 marks: Describes the leisure role of the baths with some analysis of status or community.
3 marks: Describes the baths and their facilities with limited analysis.
2 marks: Identifies one feature or use of the baths with minimal explanation.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about the baths.

sampleAnswers.answer: The public baths were central to leisure in Pompeii because they combined bathing with exercise, conversation and entertainment. The Stabian Baths, one of the oldest complexes, offered a sequence of heated, warm and cold rooms, as well as a palaestra for exercise, so that bathing was an organised routine rather than simply hygiene. Baths were places where people of different social status met, but the experience was shaped by social status: wealthy patrons could afford private access to some facilities, and their presence in the baths displayed their generosity and influence. The baths also created a sense of community, since residents gathered there for conversation, gossip and commercial dealings, and political news and local reputations were exchanged. Some complexes had separate sections for men and women, which shows that the rules of social interaction were structured. Entertainment in the baths included games, and food and drink were sold from nearby shops, so the leisure of the baths extended into the wider commercial life of the town. The baths therefore show leisure as both a private pleasure and a public institution through which social status and community ties were displayed. Bathing usually took place in the afternoon, which made the baths one of the most regular points of contact between people of different occupations and households. The palaestra and exercise areas gave young men a place to display physical skill in front of the community, so leisure was also a form of public performance.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: analyses the baths' leisure role (exercise, conversation, entertainment), the expression of social status through patronage and structured access, and the creation of community ties, with specific evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Baths in Pompeii were used for relaxing and exercise. The Stabian Baths had hot, warm and cold rooms. People went there to talk, and wealthy men could show their status. This made the baths part of the community.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate on the facilities and social functions, but the link between status, display and community is asserted rather than analysed. It fits the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: People went to the baths to wash.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement that misses the leisure, status and community roles, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student is studying the Stabian Baths and notes that one of the public bath complexes in Pompeii had separate sections for men and women. The student is asked to analyse how bathing shaped the town's leisure and social life.

dotPoints.description: Health, including diet, water supply and sanitation

prompts.question: Explain how Pompeii's water supply and sanitation systems shaped the health of the town's residents.
markerNotes: Explain needs the chain from system to health: clean water and drains reduced some diseases, while lead pipes and unequal access created new risks.
Naming the Aqua Augusta, the castellum and the lead pipes accurately earns the specific evidence mark.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that the water system made Pompeii disease-free, which the evidence does not support.
Describing the aqueduct without linking it to Augustus or to the town's supply arrangements.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains how the water supply and sanitation systems worked and assesses their effect on residents' health, including the risks of lead pipes and unequal access, with specific evidence.
4 marks: Explains the systems and their effect on health with relevant evidence and some assessment of risk.
3 marks: Describes the water supply and sanitation with limited reference to health.
2 marks: Identifies one feature of the water or sanitation system.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about Pompeii's water.

sampleAnswers.answer: The water supply of Pompeii came from the Aqua Augusta, an aqueduct that brought water from springs near Serino to a distribution tank (castellum) at the edge of the town. Lead pipes carried water from there to public fountains and some private houses, so most residents depended on fountains. The water system also made flushing latrines and drains possible, which carried waste away from the centre, so sanitation was better than in many ancient cities. However, lead pipes posed a health risk, since lead could accumulate in the body. The water supply and sanitation therefore improved the health of many residents while leaving real dangers unresolved. Benefits were also unevenly spread, since households far from the main pipes relied on public fountains. Households also collected rainwater in cisterns, so the quality of water varied with its source.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: explains how the aqueduct, castellum and lead pipes delivered water, how drains supported sanitation, and assesses the health effects, including the risk of lead and unequal access.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii had an aqueduct that brought water from the hills. Water went to fountains and some houses through pipes. There were also drains and latrines, which helped with sanitation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the system accurately, but does not explain how it affected health. It sits in the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii had running water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no system and no health link, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student is reading a summary of the water system: an aqueduct from the hills around Serino, a distribution tank at the town's edge, and lead pipes running to fountains and some houses. The student must explain how the system affected people's health.

prompts.question: Identify two foods that the organic evidence from Herculaneum shows were part of the local diet, and the type of evidence for each.
markerNotes: Two foods and the type of evidence for each are required. Naming foods alone is incomplete.
Stronger answers say what the evidence shows about diet and health, not just what the items were.
commonStudentErrors: Naming foods such as fish or olives that come from general or literary evidence, without stating the site evidence that supports them.
Confusing organic remains with art or buildings because they were found in the same houses.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies two foods, each with a correct type of evidence (for example carbonised bread or figs as organic remains).
1 mark: Identifies one food, or one type of evidence, correctly.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two foods in the diet at Herculaneum are bread and figs, each shown by organic remains: carbonised loaves and charred figs. This evidence of food shows what the diet was and supports conclusions about health.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: identifies two foods, each with a correct type of evidence (carbonised bread and charred figs as organic remains), and notes what the evidence shows about diet and health.

sampleAnswers.answer: Bread was eaten in Herculaneum.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One food with no type of evidence, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student is reading a report on carbonised food remains found at Herculaneum. The student must name two foods and the kind of evidence that supports each.

dotPoints.description: Public and private religion

prompts.question: Distinguish between public and private religion in Pompeii, using the Temple of Jupiter and household shrines as examples.
markerNotes: Distinguish needs a difference in organisation or purpose, not just two examples: civic and state-linked against domestic and personal.
The top band comes from explaining how the two levels related, for example civic cult projecting the state's authority while households kept their own devotion.
commonStudentErrors: Presenting public and private religion as entirely separate, with no link between them.
Calling the lararium a temple, which confuses household and civic religion.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Distinguishes the purpose and organisation of public religion (civic cult, magistrates, the Temple of Jupiter) from private religion (household shrines, personal devotion), using specific evidence and explaining the relationship between them.
4 marks: Distinguishes both with specific evidence and some explanation of their purpose.
3 marks: Identifies the two forms with examples but limited explanation of the difference.
2 marks: Describes one form with accurate detail.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about religion in Pompeii.

sampleAnswers.answer: Public religion in Pompeii was organised by the city's magistrates and expressed the collective identity of the community. The Temple of Jupiter, the Capitolium, stood at the northern end of the forum and was dedicated to the Capitoline triad of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, so its cult tied the town to the Roman state. Its festivals and sacrifices were paid for and overseen by the magistrates, and they reinforced civic loyalty and the authority of the office holders. Private religion, by contrast, took place in the household and reflected personal devotion. Household shrines, or lararia, were found in many houses and were used to honour the household gods, the Lares, and the family's ancestors, and offerings were made at home rather than through civic officials. Private worship also let families seek protection for their own welfare, from the harvest to the health of their members, without depending on the city's rituals. The distinction shows that religion in Pompeii operated at two levels: a public one that projected the authority of the city and the state, and a private one that gave families a direct and personal relationship with the divine. Both forms were central to the identity of the town.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: distinguishes public religion (magistrates, the Temple of Jupiter, civic loyalty) from private religion (household shrines, the Lares, personal protection), using specific evidence, and explains how the two levels related.

sampleAnswers.answer: Public religion was for the whole town and was run by magistrates. The Temple of Jupiter was an example of public religion. Private religion happened in houses with shrines that people used for their own gods.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate examples and a basic distinction, but the purpose of each level and their relationship are not explained. It sits in the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii had both public and private religion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no examples or distinction, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student is working from a plan of Pompeii's forum, where the Capitolium (a temple of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva) stands at the northern end, and from a plan of a house with a small household shrine in its kitchen area. The student must explain how the two kinds of religion differed in their organisation.

prompts.question: Describe the cult of Venus Pompeiana and what its prominence in the town reveals about religion and civic identity.
markerNotes: Describe needs the cult itself (Venus Pompeiana as patron goddess, her sanctuary) and a link to civic identity.
Marks go to the explanation of why a patron deity mattered for the town's identity.
commonStudentErrors: Treating Venus Pompeiana as a purely personal cult, when her prominence was civic.
Describing Venus as the goddess of Pompeii's trade only, without the civic role.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the cult of Venus Pompeiana, including her role as patron goddess, and explains what its prominence reveals about civic identity and religion.
2 marks: Describes the cult accurately with limited explanation.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about religion in Pompeii.

sampleAnswers.answer: Venus was worshipped in Pompeii as Venus Pompeiana, the city's patron goddess, and her cult was closely tied to civic identity. Her sanctuary and the images of Venus on public and private walls show that the goddess linked the town's religion to its self-image as a prosperous Roman community with its own distinctive protector. Public cult honoured her as the protector of the city, while private devotion appeared in household paintings and shrines, so the cult reveals the connection between religion and civic pride, and between public worship and the personal devotion of individuals. Venus was therefore a figure through whom the town expressed both its collective identity and its religious life.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: describes Venus Pompeiana as patron goddess with her sanctuary, and explains how her cult linked religion to civic identity at both public and private levels.

sampleAnswers.answer: Venus was the patron goddess of Pompeii and had a temple in the town.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate basics, but no explanation of what the cult reveals about civic identity or religion. It fits the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii worshipped many gods.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no cult named and no explanation, so only the 1-mark band applies.

dotPoints.description: The practices and challenges of excavation and conservation at the sites in the 20th and 21st centuries

prompts.question: Explain the main challenges of excavation and conservation at Pompeii and Herculaneum in the 20th and 21st centuries, and how practices have responded to them.
markerNotes: Explain needs the causal link: fragile material and visitor numbers create problems, and each conservation response carries its own trade-off.
The strongest answers show change over time, for example from earlier excavation practices to 21st-century stabilisation and management.
commonStudentErrors: Treating conservation as a 21st-century issue only, and ignoring the damage caused by early excavation.
Describing the House of the Gladiators collapse without relating it to the wider conservation problem.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains the challenges of excavation and conservation across the 20th and 21st centuries (past excavation practices, weathering, collapse, visitor pressure) and how practices have responded, with specific evidence.
4 marks: Explains the challenges and responses with relevant evidence, with some attention to change over time.
3 marks: Describes challenges with examples and limited explanation of responses.
2 marks: Identifies one challenge or response with minimal explanation.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about the sites.

sampleAnswers.answer: The challenges of excavation and conservation at Pompeii and Herculaneum have been shaped by the fragility of the material and by the scale of the sites. Early 20th-century excavation practices, including large-scale digging and the removal of objects to museums, sometimes damaged the context of finds and left exposed walls vulnerable to the weather. In the 21st century the main challenge has been the deterioration of exposed structures, which are affected by rain, heat and the sheer number of visitors, and the collapse of buildings such as the House of the Gladiators in 2010 showed how fragile some structures had become. Conservators have responded with programmes of stabilisation, improved drainage and roofing, and with funding such as the Great Pompeii Project launched in 2012, which combined repair with changed management. Herculaneum, which is partly covered by the modern town, faces different difficulties, because excavation is slower and the sites are more difficult to protect and to study. The practices of conservation therefore combine technical repair with decisions about how much of the sites to expose to the public, and each decision carries its own risks for the material.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: explains the challenges across the 20th and 21st centuries (early excavation damage, weathering, the 2010 collapse, visitor pressure), the responses (stabilisation, drainage, the Great Pompeii Project), and the trade-offs in the practices of conservation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii has had problems with weather and too many tourists. In 2010 a building called the House of the Gladiators fell down. Conservators have since tried to repair the site with new funding.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accurate examples, but the list does not discuss excavation practices or explain how the responses address the challenges. It sits in the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pompeii is difficult to look after.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no challenge, example or response, so only the 1-mark band applies.

prompts.scenario: A student is writing about the collapse of the House of the Gladiators at Pompeii in 2010 and the public debate that followed about how the sites should be managed. The student must explain both the problems and the responses.

prompts.question: Identify two conservation challenges that archaeologists at Herculaneum and Pompeii have faced in the 21st century.
markerNotes: Two challenges are needed, and each needs a brief reason. Naming a challenge without a cause earns only one mark.
Specific causes (rain and humidity, visitor wear) make the answer precise.
commonStudentErrors: Naming the 19th-century excavations as a 21st-century challenge.
Repeating one challenge in two different sentences.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies two distinct conservation challenges (for example weathering, visitor pressure, structural collapse or funding), each briefly explained.
1 mark: Identifies one challenge without explanation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two conservation challenges at Herculaneum and Pompeii are weathering, which damages exposed frescoes and mortar, and visitor pressure, which wears floors and walls. Both require conservators to balance protection with public access.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: two distinct challenges (weathering and visitor pressure), each explained with its effect on the sites, and a point about balancing protection with public access.

sampleAnswers.answer: Weather is a problem for the sites.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One challenge with no development, so only the 1-mark band applies.

dotPoints.description: Changing interpretations of the sites, including the contribution of recent technology

prompts.question: Analyse how recent technology has changed interpretations of Pompeii and Herculaneum, with reference to at least two specific techniques.
markerNotes: Analyse needs the link between technique and interpretation: radar changes what is known about the city plan, and scans change what can be read.
Naming techniques is description. The top band asks what each technique changed in the historical picture, and where it has limits.
commonStudentErrors: Claiming that technology has solved the historical questions, rather than changing the evidence available.
Naming technologies such as scanning without saying what was scanned or what was learned.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how specific techniques (such as ground-penetrating radar, LiDAR, 3D modelling and tomography of scrolls) have changed interpretations of the sites, with examples and an evaluation of their limits.
5 marks: Analyses changes in interpretation using two or more specific techniques, with some explanation of their effect.
4 marks: Describes techniques and explains their use, with some analysis of the change in interpretation.
3 marks: Describes techniques with limited analysis.
2 marks: Identifies one technique with minimal explanation.
1 mark: Makes a general statement about technology and the sites.

sampleAnswers.answer: Recent technology has produced changing interpretations of Pompeii and Herculaneum by allowing sites and objects to be studied without destructive excavation. Ground-penetrating radar and LiDAR survey have been used to map buried structures and to identify features of the urban landscape beyond the excavated areas, which has changed the view that the cities were fully known. Three-dimensional modelling and digital reconstruction allow researchers to test how light, space and movement worked in houses, and this has shifted interpretations of domestic life away from static descriptions towards dynamic accounts of use. Imaging of carbonised papyrus scrolls from the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum, using X-ray and computed tomography, has opened the possibility of reading texts that were previously unreadable, which could change understanding of the library and intellectual life of the Roman elite. Scientific analysis of organic remains and pollen also refines knowledge of diet and agriculture. Ground-level surveys of the city's drainage and water systems add to this picture, because they connect technical evidence to the everyday infrastructure described in other sources. Each technique therefore changes the evidence available, rather than simply confirming earlier conclusions. For example, the scrolls can be read only when imaging is combined with careful reconstruction of their damaged layers, which is a demanding process. These techniques show that interpretation is becoming more evidence-led, although each method has its own limitations, and changing interpretations depend on the quality of the data and the questions that historians ask.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: analyses several techniques (radar and LiDAR, 3D modelling, tomography of scrolls, scientific analysis) and what each changed in the historical picture, and evaluates the limits of the methods.

sampleAnswers.answer: New technology such as ground-penetrating radar lets archaeologists see buried parts of Pompeii without digging.
